title: Values variables and types
goals: Distinguish integer, floating-point, text and Boolean values
Trace reassignment without treating a name as a live formula
Choose a suitable representation for a count and an identifier

prerequisite.prompt: What does print(total) do after total = 24?
prerequisite.answer: It displays the current value 24. Assignment and display are separate operations.

vocabulary: A piece of data such as 8 or a text label
A name bound to a value during execution
A category of value that determines available operations
Binding an existing name to a new value

lesson.title: Choose data that matches its meaning

blocks.text: A count and a shelf label can look similar while needing different operations. The integer 8 is a number; "08" is text that preserves a leading zero. You can count eight objects, but adding two shelf labels is usually meaningless. This week you will examine values, trace changes to names and explain which representation a task needs.

Use the saved Python 3 script workflow from Week 1. Make a new file values.py, predict before running and keep actual output separately. Use fictional labels only. Four useful types are int for whole numbers, float for floating-point numbers, str for text, and bool for True or False. A type describes a value, not whether its meaning is sensible for the task.

lesson.title: Look at values and types together

blocks.text: type(count) produces the type of the value bound to count. These print lines display <class 'int'> and <class 'str'>. The quotes in "08" mark text; they are not displayed by print(shelf). True and False have capital initials and no quotes. "False" is text, not a Boolean.

blocks.title: A saved value is not a live link
blocks.caption: Evaluate the right side using the current value, then bind the left-hand name. The saved integer does not update when count is reassigned.

blocks.title: Python 3 code
blocks.text:
count = 8
saved = count
count = count + 2
print(count)
print(saved)

The outputs are 10 and 8 on separate lines. saved = count uses the value available at that moment. It does not store a formula that keeps following count. count = count + 2 is valid assignment: read the old 8, calculate 10, then rebind count. It is not a claim that 8 equals 10.

blocks.label: After count becomes 10, add saved = count and print(saved). Predict the new output and explain why this is different from expecting saved to change automatically.

lesson.title: Use an operation appropriate to the type

blocks.text: These lines display 10, 82 and 88. Number addition calculates a sum. String addition joins text; string multiplication by a whole number repeats it. Python does not infer from the digits that you wanted a number. Trying "8" + 2 instead raises TypeError because this addition mixes text and an integer.

For a supplied count, use a numeric literal such as 8. For a shelf ID, preserve text such as "08". Later weeks will parse and validate data read from files; changing a type alone will not prove that a value is valid. Use descriptive names with underscores, such as shelf_id. Names are case-sensitive: count and Count are different names.

A negative int is still an integer, but it may be invalid as a count of objects. A correctly typed label can still name the wrong shelf. Keep the task’s meaning separate from the value’s Python type. Week 3 uses arithmetic expressions and grouping to calculate with known numeric values.

blocks.label: A shelf identifier "08" is changed to the number 8 so that it can be added to another identifier. Explain what information is lost and why numeric addition does not solve an identifier task. Give one example of a value with the right type but the wrong meaning.

workbook.title: Identify the value and its type
workbook.prompt: Classify 12, 1.5, "12", False and "False". Explain why the last two are different.
workbook.answer: 12 is int; 1.5 is float; "12" is str; False is bool; "False" is str. Quotes mark text even when the characters spell a Boolean name.

workbook.title: Trace a saved value
workbook.prompt: Trace the five-line count and saved program. Record both printed outputs, then predict the result of assigning saved = count after the change. Check with a run or label a paper trace.
workbook.answer: Original outputs 10 then 8. After the new assignment, saved becomes 10. Keep actual observations separate. Reading an integer value earlier does not create a live link to another name.

workbook.title: Diagnose the operation
workbook.prompt: Predict 6 + 3, "6" + "3" and "6" * 3. Explain what happens for "6" + 3. Which expression counts six groups of three?
workbook.answer: 9, text 63, text 666, and TypeError respectively. Six groups of three needs numeric multiplication 6 * 3, giving 18; none of the listed successful expressions calculates that total.

workbook.title: Trace a new pair of names independently
workbook.prompt: A fresh script runs seats = 12; booked = seats; seats = seats - 5; print(seats); print(booked), with each statement on a separate line. Predict both outputs. Then add booked = seats + 1 and print(booked). Explain the evaluation order and choose a type for a seat label "07".
workbook.answer: The outputs are 7 and 12, then 8 after the added assignment. The right side reads the current seats value 7 before binding booked to 8. The seat label remains str to preserve its leading zero.

workbook.title: Separate type from validity
workbook.prompt: Give a suitable type for a counter count, a length of 2.5 metres, a shelf ID with a leading zero, and a yes-or-no availability flag. Give a count value with the right type that should still be rejected.
workbook.answer: Use int, float, str and bool respectively. A negative integer such as -3 has type int but is invalid for a nonnegative physical count. Type checking and checking the task’s permitted values are different.

teacher.background: Focus on scalar values and rebinding; lists and mutation come later. Avoid saying every assignment makes a deep copy. For the integers used here, rebinding one name leaves the other bound to its prior value. Reference: Python tutorial introduction, https://docs.python.org/3/tutorial/introduction.html, and built-in types, https://docs.python.org/3/library/stdtypes.html.
materials: Python 3 editor prepared in Week 1 and fresh values.py script
Name cards and value cards marked with int, float, str or bool
Fictional shelf labels and a blank trace table
sessions: Retrieve assignment versus print and collect the prerequisite.
Compare count and shelf label; model type output and complete W1.
Use the diagram and move name cards while tracing the count program.
Complete W2 with predicted and actual outputs in separate columns.
Retrieve the two saved values and explain the extra assignment in the guided task.
Run the numeric and text operations; use W3 to diagnose a TypeError.
Collect W4 independently before support, including the seat-label choice.
Complete W5 and the exit; separate type from permitted value.
teacher.guidedAnswer: The new saved = count binds saved to the current 10, so print(saved) displays 10. Without that assignment it stays 8. Exit: turning "08" into 8 loses the leading zero; identifier addition has no defined meaning in the stated task. -3 is an integer but cannot be a nonnegative count.
misconceptions: Quotes make a string, even when every character is a digit.
Changing one scalar name updates every earlier assignment
Trace the value bound at each assignment; no formula link is stored.
The right type guarantees valid data
A negative integer can be an invalid object count.
Lowercase false is Python’s Boolean false value
The literal is False; lowercase false is a name and is undefined in a fresh script.
teacher.assessment: W4 needs outputs 7, 12 and 8 with a right-side-first explanation and str for "07". After support, retry with stock = 9, spare = stock, stock = stock - 4: printing stock and spare gives 5 and 9; spare = stock + 2 then gives 7. Record independent reasoning before giving the retry.
teacher.support: Use movable name cards and immutable number cards. Keep quotations visible on text cards and show source beside output. Offer an oral trace but record assistance. Extension: explain why a type-correct number such as -3 is not acceptable as the number of seats.
teacher.next: Week 3 combines numeric values in expressions and uses parentheses to make grouping explicit.
